text.string: A story of heat, pressure and about 25 seconds
How does an espressomachine work?
Turin: Angelo Moriondo patents a steammachine that brews coffee in bulk.
Milan: Bezzera & Pavoni's 'Ideale' serves single cups,but steam only reaches about 1.5 bar.
Achille Gaggia's spring lever hits 9 bar.The golden foam on top, crema, is born.
The Faema E61 swaps muscle for an electric pump:the blueprint for modern machines.
Water is pulled from the tank
The pump squeezes it to about 9 bar
The boiler heats it to about 93 °C
Hot, pressurised water floods the coffee puck
Espresso pours out, crowned with crema
Same goal, five ways to get there
POWERED BY  YOUR ARM OR A SPRING
Pull the lever down and a spring is loaded.Let go, and the spring presses the shot.
Found in classic cafe levers and manual home machines
A magnet snaps a tiny piston back and forth50-60 times a second, pushing water in pulses.
Found in most home espresso machines

position.expression: var a = time > 1.5 ? 1 : 0; [value[0] + Math.sin(time * 95) * 2.5 * a, value[1] + Math.cos(time * 83) * 2 * a]

text.string: A motor spins a vaned disc inside an off-centrechamber, sweeping water through smoothly.
Found in cafes and high-end home setups
One button grinds, doses, tamps and brews,then dumps the used puck for you.
Found in offices and busy kitchens
POWERED BY  A SMALL VIBRATORY PUMP
A sealed capsule of ground coffee is piercedand hot water is pumped straight through it.
Found in kitchens that want coffee in seconds
Every machine trades convenience for control
Different machines.The same tiny miracle.
